title: Threadfold
subtitle: A crowdfunding platform for custom apparel, designed from nothing: design a tee, set a goal, and sell it before a single shirt is printed.

stats.label: Crowdfunding platform for custom apparel in India
Tools and vendors collapsed into one flow

overview.headline: Project Overview
overview.tldr: Threadfold was an early crowdfunding platform for custom apparel in India: design a tee in the browser, set a goal, and sell it before a single shirt is printed. I led the UX and visual redesign end to end: the Design Studio, the campaign flow, the buyer journey, and the Raiser dashboards.
overview.intro: Threadfold grew out of a college project into one of the first t-shirt crowdfunding platforms in India. National business and technology press covered it, and national children's charities ran campaigns on it. I owned the interface end to end and reframed the product as a single, cohesive platform.
overview.intro2: The redesign had one job at its center: take a process that used to span six disconnected tools and vendors, and make it feel like one calm flow that anyone could finish in an afternoon.
overview.contextBody: You publicize. We produce. You keep the profit. The creator designs and promotes; Threadfold handles production, shipping, payments and support; nobody pays upfront and nothing is printed until the campaign is funded.

primaryUsers.label: Campaign Raisers
primaryUsers.desc: Students, college clubs, bands, artists and small brands who design a tee and run a campaign to sell it, with no upfront cost and no inventory.

primaryUsers.label: Cause & NGO Raisers
primaryUsers.desc: National children's charities raising funds and awareness through merchandise campaigns.

primaryUsers.label: Buyers / Backers
primaryUsers.desc: Supporters who land on a campaign from a shared link or a Facebook ad and order the tee, which is what funds the run.

problem.headline: Selling custom merch meant juggling a stack of tools
problem.coreChallenge: To make and sell custom tees, people stitched together separate tools and vendors: one to design, another to mock it up, a printer with high minimum orders, a way to take payments, and their own shipping. Every handoff added cost, dependency and risk before a single shirt sold.

dimensions.title: A stack of disconnected tools
dimensions.desc: Design in one place, mock up in another, print with a vendor, collect payments somewhere else, arrange shipping yourself. Nothing talked to anything.

dimensions.title: Cost and risk upfront
dimensions.desc: High minimum orders and pay-first printing put real money on the line before any demand was proven.

dimensions.title: No owner of the journey
dimensions.desc: If one tool or vendor fell over, the whole campaign stalled, and the creator carried the fallout alone.

dimensions.title: Promote to strangers
dimensions.desc: Campaigns lived or died on a shareable link dropped into Facebook ads and social, so the funnel had to convert cold traffic.

problem.hypothesis: If one platform owns the entire journey, design, pricing, payments, production, shipping and payout, then a creator can launch with zero upfront cost and nothing to wrangle but the idea.

howItWorks.headline: How a campaign works
howItWorks.intro: I surfaced the whole product as one loop, right on the homepage, so a first-time raiser gets it before they ever sign up.

steps.d: Pick a product and color, drop in artwork, text or an upload, and preview it live on the tee. A base cost appears instantly for different quantities.
Choose a sales goal, an end date and a per-tee price; the flow shows the minimum profit before you launch. Share the campaign link and drive traffic with Facebook ads and social.
If the goal is met, Threadfold prints, ships to every buyer, and transfers the profit. The raiser pays nothing upfront and nothing if the campaign falls short, so there is no inventory and no risk.

image.caption: Homepage: the model explained to a first-time raiser, with live campaigns and press credibility.

ia.headline: Structuring a stack of tools into one platform
ia.intro: The IA had to hold a creator tool, a public storefront, and a back office in one place, none of them feeling bolted on. So I organized everything around three jobs: create a campaign, back a campaign, and manage what you have launched.
ia.caption: Information architecture: the creator studio, the buyer storefront, and the raiser back office under one roof.

userFlow.headline: One journey, two sides
userFlow.intro: I split the journey in two so neither side carries the other's weight. The raiser designs, prices and launches. The buyer arrives from an ad or a shared link and orders. Everything in between, production, payments, shipping, is the platform's job, not theirs.
userFlow.caption: The raiser and buyer journeys, meeting at the live campaign page.

wireframes.headline: From graybox layouts to the final product
wireframes.intro: Before any visual design, I blocked out the heaviest screens in grayscale to settle structure and hierarchy. Each one was a few layout options pressure-tested on its core job.

batches.caption: Design Studio: controls in a left rail vs a top toolbar vs floating panels. The left rail won, keeping the live tee preview central.
Set Price and Goal: economics buried in a form vs surfaced as a live profit panel beside the tee. The live panel made the money obvious before launch.
Homepage: explain-then-browse vs browse-first vs a single hero. Explain-then-browse won, since most visitors had never seen crowdfunded tees.

studio.headline: The Design Studio: design in the browser, nothing to install
studio.intro: Instead of opening design software, exporting a file and emailing a printer, a creator designs right here. Pick a product and color, then add artwork, a layout, text, an upload or a background, with a live preview and a running base cost. It's one step inside a single flow that ends in a live campaign, not a handoff to the next tool.

image.caption: Design Studio: central live preview, one controls rail, and base cost surfaced as you design.

points.d: Design in the browser. The file never leaves the platform on its way to print, so there is nothing to export, email or re-upload.
Front and back, real product colors, and a curated artwork library so a blank tee becomes a finished design fast.
A base cost at a sample quantity sits beside the canvas, so the economics start before the campaign flow even opens.

campaign.headline: Making the money obvious
campaign.intro: Design is step one of three: Design your tee, Set your price, Add a description. The pricing step is where most platforms hide the economics; I pulled them into the open. A goal slider, an end date and a per-tee price update a live minimum-profit figure. The reassurance that matters most, pay nothing even if the campaign fails, sits right beside the CTA.

screens.title: Set Your Price
screens.desc: Goal slider, campaign end date and selling price update a live minimum-profit figure; the no-risk promise sits beside the CTA.

screens.title: Add a Description
screens.desc: The final step before launch, the story and details that make a campaign shareable.

screens.title: Campaign Page
screens.desc: The public campaign page a raiser shares into Facebook ads and social to convert cold traffic into buyers.

dashboard.headline: Running the campaign after launch
dashboard.intro: Once a campaign is live, the raiser needs to track orders, watch the goal, manage their account, and get paid. I kept the dashboards in the same calm, single-focus language as the studio, so going live never felt like switching to a different product.

screens.title: Order Tracking
screens.desc: Where a raiser follows orders and campaign progress at a glance.

screens.title: Payout
screens.desc: The profit transfer view, the moment the whole model pays off for the creator.

screens.title: Stories
screens.desc: Real campaigns and causes, doubling as social proof for the next raiser.

screens.title: Account
screens.desc: Profile and settings, kept light so the focus stays on creating and selling.

responsive.headline: Desktop to mobile
responsive.intro: I designed the studio and storefront to scale from a wide desktop canvas down to a single-column phone layout. On mobile the model collapses to the same three promises: Design in Minutes, Set Your Price and Sell, We Produce You Profit. So a campaign discovered on a phone, where most ad traffic landed, still makes sense in one scroll.

reflection.headline: What it was, and what I'd do differently
reflection.note: I won't invent numbers for this one. What stands is the work itself and what the press recorded at the time.
press: One of the first crowdfunding platforms for t-shirts and custom apparel in India.
Covered by national newspapers and the technology and startup press.
Used for college tees, fan groups, artwork and social causes, including campaigns run with national children's charities.
Reported by press to have grown quickly through 2014 and 2015.
differently: The Design Studio tried to offer everything at once. I'd stage the controls harder, getting a raiser to a sellable design in three taps and revealing power later.
We designed desktop-first; most ad traffic arrived on phones. I'd lead with the mobile campaign flow next time, not retrofit it.
The economics UI was strong but untested with real raisers. I'd put the goal, price and profit screen in front of actual first-time creators before build.
Campaign pages had to convert cold Facebook traffic, a job for sharper, test-driven landing pages than a one-size template.

deck.standfirst: Selling a custom tee meant six tools, a printer with minimums, and your own money on the line. We built the thing that replaced all of it, starting from a blank page and a risky assumption.

assumptions.title: I did not start with screens. I started with what could kill this.
bullets: The model only works if a chain of beliefs all hold, and most of them had **no evidence behind them at all**. So the first job was writing them down and sorting them by what happens if they are wrong.
Importance on one axis, evidence on the other. Everything in the top-left corner is a bet the business dies on, with nothing supporting it yet.
Three landed there. **Creators will promote their own campaign.** **Buyers will pay for a shirt that does not exist yet.** **Buyers will trust an unknown site with their card.**
The first one is the whole company. Threadfold has no audience of its own: every sale comes through a link the creator shares. If creators do not promote, nothing else on this page matters.
So that became the thing to design for, and the thing to test first, before a single interface decision got made.
shot: Assumption map: importance against evidence, with the three that got tested first
assumptions.how: A two-hour workshop with the two founders and the engineer. Everyone wrote beliefs on cards alone first, so the loudest person in the room did not set the list, and we ended up with 31 of them. Placing each card was the argument: importance was quick to agree on, evidence was not, and every time somebody said "we know that" I asked how we knew. Most of those cards moved left. The three that ended up top-left got a test each before I opened a design tool.

research.title: Two user groups, and no way to study them the same way.
bullets: Creators were few, findable and generous with time. Buyers were many, anonymous, and gone in ninety seconds. Running the same method on both would have meant doing one of them badly.

So creators got depth: **nine contextual inquiry sessions** in their own rooms and hostels, watching them try to make a design with the tools they already had. Four kept a diary through a live campaign.
Buyers got breadth: **340 intercept survey responses** off live campaigns, plus five-second tests on the campaign page to find out what a stranger takes away before they decide to scroll.

I also made a sequencing call here. Roughly **two-thirds of failed marketplaces die on the supply side**, not demand, so creators got the deep research and the first release. Buyers got a page that converts and not much else.
shot: The research plan: few and deep on the supply side, many and shallow on the demand side
research.how: Creators were recruited through college notice boards and two student bands, and I went to them rather than making them come to us, because the point was to see the laptop and the half-finished poster on it. Sessions ran about an hour, task-based, watching them try to make a design with whatever they already used. Buyers were intercepted on live campaign pages with a three-question exit survey, which is the only honest way to reach someone who was never going to sit down with me.

findings: Nobody could picture the finished thing

Every creator I sat with described the same block: they could imagine the design and they could imagine wearing it, and nothing in between. Sketching on paper did not help because paper is not a t-shirt. This is why the live preview is the centre of the studio and not a step at the end.
The money question came first, not last

I expected creativity questions. I got "what do I make on this?" in the first five minutes of seven out of nine sessions. Pricing was not a boring form to get through. It was the thing they were actually deciding.
"I do not want to ask my friends for money"

The riskiest assumption cracked here. Creators would happily share something they had made; they would not run a fundraiser. So the product had to feel like selling a product, not soliciting donations, which changed the language on every screen.
Buyers were not backing a cause, they were buying a shirt
The survey was blunt about it. Most buyers described the purchase as buying a tee from someone they knew. The crowdfunding mechanic mattered to them only as a reason it might not arrive.
deck.findingsHow: Two of us affinity-mapped the session notes independently before comparing, which is slower but stops one person's pet theory becoming the finding. Anything only one of us had seen got flagged rather than dropped, and the buyer survey was coded separately so a strong creator quote could not colour how the buyer data read.

blueprint.title: A journey map would have shown me half the product.
bullets: The promise here is "we produce, you profit". Everything in the second half of that sentence, printing, quality checks, packing, courier, payment capture, payout, is **invisible to both users**.
A journey map captures what the two people do and feel. It cannot show you the thing that makes or breaks this service, which is what the business does underneath them.
So I blueprinted it: physical evidence, creator actions, buyer actions, then the **line of visibility**, then everything backstage and the systems supporting it.

Two things fell out of it immediately. The creator has **nothing to do** between the goal being hit and the money arriving, which is a silence long enough to lose trust in. And **payment is held rather than captured** until the goal is met, which is the mechanic the no-risk promise is actually made of, and nowhere in the UI said so.
Both of those became interface work: a status the creator can watch during the silent stretch, and plain language about the held payment next to the buy button.
shot: Service blueprint: the frontstage above the line of visibility, and the production chain below it
blueprint.how: I walked one real order end to end and wrote down every step, including the ones that happened in a WhatsApp group rather than in software. Then I sat with operations and the print partner and mapped it on a wall in lanes, working downward: what the two users see, then what we do that they never see, then the systems underneath. Both problems it surfaced were gaps in the lanes rather than on the screens, which is exactly why a journey map would have missed them.

iaMethod.title: The first structure was ours, not theirs.
bullets: I had grouped the navigation the way we talked about the product internally, which is the most common way to get this wrong.
**48 participants sorted 34 content cards.** What came back grouped around what people were trying to do rather than which part of the company owned it.
Tree testing the original structure gave **52% task success**, well under the 75% that counts as a working navigation. Regrouped around three jobs, create, back, manage, it went to **81%**.

First-click testing then checked the visual implementation, moving correct first clicks from **44% to 78%**. That matters more than it sounds: a correct first click makes someone roughly **three times more likely to finish the task at all**.
shot: Card sort into tree test into first-click test, with the before and after
iaMethod.how: An open card sort, run remotely so people grouped and named things without me in the room nudging the vocabulary. I then rebuilt the resulting tree as a bare text hierarchy with no visual design on it at all and set real tasks against it, so the only thing under test was whether the labels and grouping made sense. First-click testing came last, on actual screens, because that measures the visual implementation rather than the structure.

testing: The first studio was a step-by-step wizard: pick product, then colour, then artwork, then text. Creators hated being told the order. Four of five backed out at the colour step to go and find artwork first. The studio became a single canvas with a controls rail, and nothing enforcing sequence.

Pricing sat on its own screen, after the design. Creators reached the price step, discovered their margin was thin, and went back to change the design, which meant losing work. The base cost moved into the studio, live, next to the canvas.

"No risk" tested as marketing noise. People did not believe it and could not say what it meant. Rewritten as the mechanic itself, that nobody is charged unless the goal is met, it stopped being a claim and started being an explanation.
Round four was the buyer's turn

With creators settled I ran the buyer side properly. Forced account creation before checkout lost people outright, which matches the ecommerce research: it is the second most common reason carts get abandoned, at 24%. Guest checkout went in and the field count came down from 21 to 13.

That was the signal to stop. Five participants per side per round, which is the sample where new findings dry up for a homogeneous group, and with two distinct groups that meant ten people a round rather than five.
deck.testingHow: Moderated and task-based, in person for creators and remote for buyers. I gave people a goal rather than a script ("get to a design you would put your name on") and then stayed quiet, timing where they stalled. Each round changed one structural thing, so the next round tested that change rather than a new product. The round-five stop rule was written before round one, so ending it was a decision made in advance rather than when I got tired.

problem.statement: To sell a custom tee you had to be your own production manager: design somewhere, mock it up somewhere else, find a printer with a minimum order, take payments yourself, and arrange the shipping. Every handoff added cost and risk before a single shirt sold.
bullets: **A stack of disconnected tools.** Design in one place, mock up in another, print with a vendor, collect payments somewhere else, ship it yourself. Nothing talked to anything.
**Money on the line first.** High minimum orders and pay-before-print meant real cash committed before any demand was proven.
**Nobody owned the journey.** One vendor falling over stalled the whole campaign, and the creator carried it alone.
**Cold traffic only.** Campaigns lived or died on a link dropped into a Facebook ad, so the funnel had to convert strangers.

bet.title: One platform owns everything, so the creator only owns the idea.
bullets: If design, pricing, payments, production, shipping and payout all sit in one place, the creator has nothing left to wrangle.
And if nothing is printed until the campaign funds, the upfront cost goes to **zero** and the risk moves off the creator entirely.
That is the whole product in one sentence: **you publicise, we produce, you keep the profit**.
My job was to make a first-time visitor believe that in one scroll, then walk them through it without a handoff.

twoSides.title: Two journeys that only meet at the campaign page.
bullets: The raiser designs, prices and launches. The buyer arrives from an ad or a shared link and orders.
Neither should carry the other's weight, so I split the flows and let them meet at exactly one place.
Everything between the two, production, payments and shipping, is the platform's job and stays off both screens.

ia.title: A creator tool, a shop and a back office under one roof.
bullets: The hard part of the architecture was that none of the three could feel bolted on to the other two.
So I organised it around three jobs rather than three products: **create a campaign, back a campaign, manage what you launched**.
That is why going live never feels like switching apps. It is the same vocabulary either side of the launch button.

wireframes: Design Studio: left rail, top toolbar, or floating panels. The rail won because it keeps the live tee central.
Set price: economics buried in a form, or surfaced beside the tee. Surfaced won.
Homepage: explain first, browse first, or a single hero. Explain first won, because almost nobody had seen a crowdfunded tee.

dives.title: Nothing to install, and the file never leaves the platform.
bullets: The old way started by opening design software and ended by emailing a printer. This starts and ends in the browser.
Pick a product and colour, then add artwork, text, an upload or a background, with the tee updating live in the middle of the screen.
Front and back, real product colours, and a curated artwork library, so a blank tee becomes something sellable fast.
A **base cost sits beside the canvas** while you design. The economics start before the campaign flow even opens.
shot: Design Studio: live tee preview in the centre, one controls rail, base cost always visible

dives.title: Most platforms hide the economics. I put them on the screen.
bullets: Pricing is the step where a first-time creator decides whether this is worth doing, so burying it in a form was never going to work.
A goal slider, an end date and a per-tee price drive a **live minimum-profit figure** that moves as you move them.
The reassurance that actually matters, that you pay nothing if the campaign falls short, sits next to the launch button rather than in a help page.
Three steps total: design the tee, set the price, add the description. Then it is live and shareable.
shot: Set your price: goal, end date and price driving a live minimum-profit figure

dives.title: The back office speaks the same language as the studio.
bullets: Once a campaign is running the raiser needs four things: track orders, watch the goal, manage the account, and get paid.
I kept all of it in the same calm single-focus layout as the studio, so launching never feels like being handed to a different product.
The payout view is the moment the model pays off for the creator, so it is the plainest screen in the set. No cleverness anywhere near someone's money.
shot: Payout: the moment the model pays off, deliberately the plainest screen in the product

responsive.title: Most of the traffic arrived on a phone.
bullets: Campaigns were promoted through Facebook ads and shared links, which meant the majority of first impressions happened on a small screen.
So the studio and the storefront both scale from a wide desktop canvas down to a single column.
On mobile the model collapses to the same three promises in one scroll: design in minutes, set your price, we produce and you profit.
This is also the thing I would do differently. We designed desktop-first and adapted down. The traffic said we had it backwards.

differently.title: Four things I would do differently, and one I would keep.
bullets: **The studio offered too much at once.** I would stage the controls harder and get a raiser to a sellable design in three taps, revealing the power later.
**We designed desktop-first and the traffic was mobile.** I would lead with the phone campaign flow rather than retrofitting it.
**The economics screen was never tested with real raisers.** It was the strongest idea in the product and the least validated, which is a bad combination.
**Campaign pages needed to be landing pages.** Converting cold ad traffic is its own discipline and a one-size template was not it.
**What I would keep: putting the money on the screen.** Every instinct in commerce design says hide the pricing mechanics. Surfacing them is what made the model believable.
